activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: Over the past century, U.S. stocks have earned higher average yearly returns than U.S. government bonds, but with much bigger drops along the way; the extra return rewards the extra risk.
story:
Lauren's Saturday job at the plant shop paid eight dollars an hour, but the real compensation was the back room, where Ms. Carvalho let her tape the investing-game leaderboard to the freezer. The whole class had split into a stock team and a bond team, and every Monday Ms. Carvalho read out the totals while Lex drummed on his desk.

Lauren was on the bond team with Aubrey, and for the first month they had led. Then the stock team had pulled ahead by so much that Lex wore a paper crown to science class. Then came a week when the stock team's number dropped like a dropped tray of seedlings, and the bonds barely wobbled, and Lauren's team was back on top. Then the stocks climbed again. She wrote the totals on the back of a rose receipt: eleven dollars, then minus six, then nine. Up and down, up and down, and somehow by June the stock team was ahead overall, again.

She was still staring at the receipt when Aubrey came in to buy potting soil and ended up repotting a fern instead, because Aubrey had never once left the shop with only what she came for. "They're winning and losing at the same time," Lauren said. "That's the part nobody says out loud." She smoothed the receipt flat on the freezer. "Their good weeks are better than ours. Their bad weeks are worse than anything we've ever had. Add it all up across the whole game, and they're ahead."

"So we lose," Aubrey said, dirt to her elbows.

"No. Now we know something." Lauren decided to test it. She asked Ms. Carvalho, who was squashing a rebellious mint that had escaped its pot and gone sideways across the shelf, whether she could integrate the old game records from the last few years into one long chart. Ms. Carvalho found a folder, sneezed twice from the dust, and left her to it. The chart took two Saturdays and a lot of freezer tape. Every past game showed the same shape: bonds crawling along in a nearly flat line, stocks leaping and dropping and leaping, and by the end, every single time, the stocks finished higher.

Lauren copied the shape onto an index card and brought it to class. Lex looked at it, then at his crown, which he had stopped wearing. "So the extra points are like a prize," he said slowly, "for taking the extra falls."

"For surviving them," Lauren said. Ms. Carvalho started the next round, and Lauren slid her chair closer to the stock team's side of the room.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Rinsing rice before cooking washes off loose surface starch, which helps the cooked grains stay separate instead of sticky.
story:
Grace had never cooked a whole meal before, and she had chosen the hardest possible night to start. Alyson's parents would be home at half past six, which gave the girls exactly fifty minutes to produce rice, a curry, and flatbread that all arrived at the table together. Alyson's kitchen smelled of toasted spices, and the curry was already bubbling, darker and richer than anything Grace had expected to make on her first try.

"Start the rice now," Alyson said, tapping the recipe on her phone. "It takes the longest." Grace measured the basmati into the pot, added water, and set it on the burner while she mixed flour and water for the flatbread dough. She had learned about polymers in science that week, long chains of molecules that made things stretch, and she thought of it as she kneaded, feeling the dough turn from shaggy to smooth under her palms.

When she lifted the rice lid to check, her stomach dropped. The grains had clumped into a single pale mass, glued together in thick streaks. "It's sticky," she said, poking it with a fork. "It's ruined." She remembered, suddenly, the last time she had tried to cook something on her own, the pancakes she had abandoned halfway through and scraped into the bin. Her mom hadn't scolded her, which somehow felt worse.

Alyson leaned over the pot. "Did you rinse it?" Grace blinked. She hadn't. She hadn't even considered it. Alyson shrugged. "Rinsing washes off the loose surface starch. That's why the grains stay separate instead of sticky." Grace stared at the gluey pot, thinking it through. The starch was on the outside of the grain, so washing before cooking could carry it away, and what was gone couldn't glue anything. It was a rule she couldn't see working, hidden inside the pot, but it made sense of what she was looking at. There was no time for regret. She filled the pot again, measured fresh rice, and swirled water through it three times until the water ran almost clear.

"New batch," she said. "We'll cook it on high while I roll the flatbread." She worked fast, dusting the counter with flour, pressing the dough into flat rounds. The curry hissed and thickened; the second pot of rice steamed with a smell like clean rain. When the timer went off, Grace lifted the lid and there it was, each grain standing apart, loose and separate. Alyson's parents walked in at 6:29 as the flatbread puffed on the hot pan, and Alyson pointed at the pot of rice and said, "Look. She fixed it."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Italian tempo words describe speed: largo means very slow, andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively.
story:
The band room smelled like floor wax and old valve oil, and the radiator by the window ticked as it warmed up. Layla sat at the second piano bench with the duet score open between her and Elizabeth. Ms. Sadeghi had written a sticky note on the front page: "Spring Concert, two weeks. Watch your tempo markings." Layla ran her pencil down the page. The first section said largo, the middle said andante, and the last said allegro.

"Okay, ready?" Elizabeth set her hands on the keys. "Largo first." They started, and the opening came out slow and heavy, like a boat drifting through deep water. Layla loved that part. Then the word andante appeared above the next section, and she leaned over and whispered, "This one's fast, right? It looks like a fast word." Elizabeth shrugged, and Layla dove in at speed. Her fingers tangled over Elizabeth's left hand, the melody crashed into the accompaniment, and they stopped three measures later with a dissonant chord hanging in the air like a wet coat.

"Whatever that was," Elizabeth said, "it wasn't it."

That night Layla sat at the kitchen table and found a message in her email from Georgia, who had moved away in the fall but still practiced piano. Georgia wrote: "Mom says my great-aunt used to sing opera, and she left us a stack of old sheet music with Italian words everywhere. Guess what my mom told me when I asked. Allegro means fast and lively. Andante means at a walking pace. Largo means very slow. These Italian words describe speed. Write back and tell me your piece actually sounds good now."

Layla sat back. A walking pace. She had been sprinting through a section that wanted a stroll. It reminded her of the summer she learned to make bread with her grandmother, who kept saying, "Slow makes flavor," and wouldn't let her turn the oven up no matter how impatient she got. Rushing had ruined that bread, and rushing had just ruined the duet. Her dilemma now was simple: how to make the change from largo to andante feel like a real transition instead of a stumble.

The next morning she arrived early and found Elizabeth already at the piano. "Georgia emailed me," Layla said. "Andante means at a walking pace. And allegro means fast and lively, so that's the sprint at the end. Largo stays very slow." She set a metronome on the lid and tapped out a walking beat, then played the opening largo, counted silently, and let her hands settle into the new tempo. The gradual shift worked like a door opening instead of a wall falling down.

By Thursday they could run the whole piece, and when Ms. Sadeghi stopped by the doorway with her coffee, she listened through half of it and smiled without saying a word. At the allegro, Layla lifted her hands, and Elizabeth counted, "One, two, ready, go."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: In Islam, barzakh, an Arabic word for barrier, is the stage the soul passes through between a person's death and the resurrection.
story:
Juliette had been to her own church exactly four hundred times, probably, but she had never set foot inside a mosque until the day of the interfaith open house. Her classmate Octavia had invited her, and Juliette, who kept a notebook of questions she was too embarrassed to ask out loud, had written three of them on her hand in pen before leaving the house. The first one was small and specific: do they have stained glass? The answer, she discovered within a minute, was no. The second question was bigger.

"My grandpa's buried near here," Octavia said as they stood in the courtyard, where the arches rose in pale curves overhead. "We visit him on Fridays." She pointed through the gate toward the cemetery next door, rows of simple stones, no carvings, no crosses, only names and dates. Juliette felt the third question on her palm start to itch.

"Where do you think he is now?" Juliette asked. She tried to make it sound like the kind of thing you could just wonder about, out loud, on a Saturday. Octavia didn't look offended. She looked like she had been waiting for someone to ask.

"In barzakh," Octavia said. "It's an Arabic word for barrier. It's the stage the soul passes through between a person's death and the resurrection." She said it plainly, like reciting a recipe she'd made a hundred times, and Juliette copied it into her notebook with the pen from her jacket, determined not to let a single word drop.

Later, in the quiet hall where visitors were invited to sit, Juliette dismantled her question into pieces the way she did with math problems. A barrier. Between death and something after it. She thought about her own grandmother's funeral, the hymn about sleeping and waking, the pastor's words about a kingdom that had no map. Both faiths had drawn a line through time, she noticed, and both had put something on the far side of it. She tested the idea out loud, hesitant, watching Octavia's face for the flicker that meant she'd gotten it wrong. "So both of them say death isn't the end. It's like a door with a hallway after it."

Octavia considered this, tapping her shoe against the tile. "A really long hallway," she said. "But yeah. A hallway." Then she grabbed Juliette's sleeve and pulled her toward the front, where a man was unfolding a carpet patterned in green and gold, and said, "You have to see this part."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Medicines and cleaning products should be kept up high and out of reach, because young children explore by putting things in their mouths.
story:
Tristan had memorized three rules from Ms. Bélanger before she left for her meeting: crackers are in the cupboard, the sippy cup is in the fridge, and do not fall asleep before eight. Her daughter, Martine, was two, and Martine's current mission in life was to put every object on Earth into her mouth.

"You can't eat that," Tristan told her, plucking a rubber duck from her jaws. He set it on the coffee table, and Martine watched it go with the narrowed eyes of a general planning a second campaign.

That was when he noticed the little bottle sitting beside the duck. It was orange, childproof, and full of white vitamins, and it was sitting low enough that Martine could reach it by simply leaning over and grabbing it. Tristan picked it up and turned it over in his hands. Ms. Bélanger was the most careful person on the street; she labeled her recycling bins and alphabetized her spice rack. So why was this down here? He thought it through. Probably she had taken her vitamin this morning and set the bottle down, meaning to put it away later, and then forgotten. That was plausible. It was also, he realized, exactly how accidents happened. Medicines and cleaning products were supposed to be kept up high and out of reach, because young children explored by putting things in their mouths, and Martine was the chief explorer of the entire tundra of the living room carpet.

He swept the room like a detective. Under the sink he found a spray bottle of cleaner behind a bucket, low and reachable once Martine mastered doorknobs, which she was clearly working on. He carried it to the top of the fridge, then climbed a chair to put the vitamins on the highest shelf of the kitchen cupboard. Martine followed him the whole way, yelling "Up! Up!" and pointing at the chair as if to disclose his crime.

"Nope," Tristan said. "Up is exactly the point."

At eight his friend Frederique texted: "How's the baby? Need backup?" Tristan sent back a photo of Martine asleep in her blanket fort, one arm flung over the rubber duck.

"Terrible," he wrote. "She defeated me at blocks twice."

When Ms. Bélanger came home, she found him on the couch, wide awake, with a note on the coffee table: "Vitamins on top shelf, cleaner on fridge. Ask me why." She read it, looked at the cupboard, then at Martine, and pressed a hand to her mouth.

"You," she said, "are hired forever."

"Benefits include crackers," Tristan said, and pointed at the cupboard.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Spanish, a la derecha means to the right, but derecho, as in sigue derecho, means keep going straight, and learners often confuse the two.
story:
Nicolas spread the Spanish worksheet across the library table and glared at it like it had personally insulted him. "It's one word," he whispered to Emmie. "Derecho, derecha. The test is Thursday, and I keep mixing them up."

"Then don't mix them up," Emmie said, not looking up from her book.

"Wow. Brilliant. Why didn't I think of that?"

She kicked him under the table, which was fair.

Rocco slid into the third chair with a fistful of flashcards and news. "Guess what. Ms. Lavoie's cousin is a train conductor in Madrid, and he's video-calling her fifth-period Spanish class tomorrow. She said if we can ask for and understand directions by then, we get to talk to him. In Spanish."

"Both ways?" Nicolas said. "Ask and understand the answer?"

"That's the whole point, apparently." Rocco fanned the cards. "So. Sigue derecho."

"Sigue right," Nicolas said confidently.

"Sigue derecho," Rocco repeated, and something about his flat tone made Nicolas stop.

"Wait." Nicolas pulled the worksheet closer. The exercise map showed a street with a bank on the left and a bakery straight ahead at the end. The answer key said sigue derecho led to the bakery. He traced the route with his pencil, straight down the avenue, past the bank, to the pastries. Then he flipped to the matching problem. A la derecha, said the prompt, and the key arrow swung right, toward a fountain that wasn't even on the main street.

He sat back. "They're not the same word. Derecho means keep going straight. Derecha, with the a in front, means to the right." He said it out loud twice, then once more, tapping the pencil. "That's why the traveller in the workbook turned right and ended up at the fountain instead of the bakery. He heard derecho and thought derecha."

"Give me that," Emmie said, finally interested. She read the map, read the key, and slid it back. "You're right. Which means every time you said it backwards in class on Monday, you sent people the wrong way."

"Don't remind me." Monday had been the most humiliating three minutes of his life. He'd stood at the front, pointed confidently, and directed half the class toward the storage closet while insisting it was the office. Ms. Lavoie had watched with the patience of someone grading papers in her head.

Now he grabbed a blank card. On one side he wrote SIGUE DERECHO and drew a long arrow, straight as a train track. On the other he wrote A LA DERECHA with an arrow bending hard right. "Rocco, quiz me. Fast. The conductor call is tomorrow and my Spanish reputation is currently endangered."

Rocco held up a card. "El banco?"

"Keep going straight. Sigue derecho."

"La fuente?"

"Right. A la derecha." Nicolas grabbed the next card before Rocco even lifted it. "Faster. We've got pastries to find and trains to catch."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect.
story:
Nicholas stood at the back lab table with three paper airplanes lined up like jets waiting for takeoff. Zack leaned over them, frowning. "You folded all three different ways," Zack said. "One has wide wings, one has skinny wings, and that one is basically a dart."

"That's the point," Nicholas said. Tomorrow was the science fair, and he still didn't have a board, only a notebook full of flight distances that made no sense. Wide wings had flown 4 meters, then 7, then 3. Skinny wings had gone 9 meters and then nosedived into Mr. Yip's sink. He had changed the wing shape, but he had also thrown them harder on some tries, and from different spots, and once the window fan had been on. His data looked like it came from a counterfeit experiment, real paper and real numbers hiding a mess underneath.

Julius walked over with his own project, a maze for his hamster, and watched Nicholas hurl the dart plane into the counter. "You're doing it wrong," Julius said. "Mr. Yip drilled us on this in September. The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose."

"And the dependent variable is what you measure to see the effect," Nicholas finished slowly. He looked at his planes again. He had changed wing shape, throwing force, launch height, and room wind, all at once. His experiment was rebelling against him because he'd never told it what to change. "I need one thing different," he said. "Wing shape. Everything else stays exactly the same."

Mr. Yip was watering the fern by the window, and Nicholas asked if he could borrow masking tape and stay through lunch. He taped a line on the floor, marked a launch spot, and made Zack promise to throw every plane with the same smooth motion. "Like I have an allergy to extra force," Zack said, rolling his eyes, but he did it. Nicholas wrote down each flight without letting himself pick favorites.

By the last bell the wide-wing plane had won four out of five throws, its longest flight skimming past the skeleton in the corner and landing on the radiator. Skinny wings averaged less than half that distance, and the data finally made a pattern he could graph. Julius helped him title the board, WING SHAPE AND FLIGHT DISTANCE, and Zack carried it to the gym with the tape still stuck to his sneaker. At the door, Nicholas turned back for the planes, folded the winner carefully in half, and slid it into his backpack like a trophy.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Robert Hooke named cells in his 1665 book Micrographia after seeing tiny compartments in a thin slice of cork under his microscope.
story:
Samuel held the tweezers too tightly and tore the onion skin for the third time. "You're being aggressive with it," Aniyah said, peeling her own sliver of skin off the onion half. "Lay it flat and let go." Samuel tried again. This time the skin came off in a thin, wobbly sheet, and he smoothed it onto his slide and added one drop of iodine, the way the directions on the board said.

Mr. Rao had shown them how to calibrate the microscope first, clicking the lowest lens into place before they were allowed anywhere near the fine focus knob. Samuel turned the stage knobs slowly, and the blurry purple haze sharpened into shapes he recognized at once. Little boxes, pressed together like bricks in a wall. His stomach did a small jump. It looked exactly like a drawing he had seen at the science museum in October, in a glass case near the exit: a copy of Robert Hooke's drawing from 1665, a slice of cork broken into tiny rooms. He had stood there for a long time because the picture looked like something from a comic, and then read the card twice.

"Mr. Rao," Samuel called, "Hooke's drawing, from Micrographia. Is that what this is?" Mr. Rao came over and leaned to Samuel's eyepiece. "Hooke saw those compartments in a thin slice of cork under his microscope," he said, "and he named them cells, right there in the book." Samuel wrote cells in his margin, then looked back at the slide. Hooke had only seen the walls, the boxes. But the lab sheet wanted three labels: cell wall, membrane, and nucleus. The nucleus was the problem. All Samuel could see were edges.

He thought about it while Aniyah took her turn. If the wall was the box, the nucleus had to be inside the box, something round, probably darker because the iodine stained it. Maybe he had torn off layers that were too thick, and the round thing was buried. He took a fresh slide and pulled the skin from a different, thinner layer of the onion, close to the flat side. Aniyah watched him do it and copied him. Marshall, at the next table, leaned over. "Why'd you change layers?" "Hooke only saw the outside of his boxes," Samuel said. "I want the inside."

Under the lens, the new slide showed the same brick walls, but now there was a small dark dot floating near the center of several boxes, plain as a pencil mark. Samuel labeled it nucleus, then drew the membrane as the faint line just inside each wall. He checked the museum memory against his own drawing: same boxes, plus the parts Hooke's cork never showed. Marshall peered into Samuel's eyepiece and said, "It's really in there. Like a dot in every single one."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: The 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right.
story:
The regional spelling bee was held in the gymnasium of a school two towns over, and the bus ride took forty minutes. Cameron sat near the window with his word list on his knee, mouthing letters while Demi and Jaiden argued about whether the driver would let them eat the granola bars hidden in Jaiden's backpack. Cameron barely heard them. He had come second last year, losing on the word "rhinoceros" after he swapped the letters s and o at the very end, and the memory still made his ears hot.

In the flashback he kept having, he stood at the microphone in the library while the vice principal read the word, and he could see his mother in the second row mouthing breathe, Cameron, breathe. He had spelled it confidently, too, which was the worst part. He had been sure. The bell had buzzed, and a girl named Priya had won with "chandelier," and Cameron had smiled at her with his face while his stomach dropped like an elevator with cut cables.

"You're doing the thing," Demi said, poking his arm. "The stare-at-nothing thing."

"I keep thinking about losing," Cameron admitted.

Jaiden leaned across the aisle. "Did you know the big national one, the Scripps bee, once ended with eight co-champions? My cousin told me. Everybody kept spelling everything right, so eight people shared the title." He shrugged. "So even the best spellers in the country, nobody could knock anybody out."

Cameron turned that over. He had been imagining the bee as a narrow doorway that only one person could fit through, and himself jammed against the frame while someone else slid through. But if a whole national bee could end with eight winners, then the doorway was wider than he had pictured. If two spellers never missed, they could both stand at the top. Being unbeatable mattered more than beating somebody.

He tested the idea out loud, because saying things was how he checked them. "So if I get every word right and the other kid gets every word right, we could both win?"

"That's what my cousin said," Jaiden answered. "Eight of them. In 2019."

The bus hissed to a stop in front of the other school, and the spellers lined up in the aisle. Ms. Bélanger, who had ridden along as the coach, gave Cameron a nod as he passed. Inside the gym, the microphone waited on the stage, and the pronouncer shuffled her cards. Cameron sat in row three with his hands folded, his mind running over patterns like a laser cutting a clean line through steel. When sophisticated came up in the practice round, he nailed it without hesitating, all four s sounds in their proper places. Then his own first word arrived.

"Your word is advocate," the pronouncer said.

"A-D-V-O-C-A-T-E," said Cameron. "Advocate."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, where bones lengthen during childhood; a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows.
story:
The waiting room smelled like antiseptic and cold coffee, and Brooklyn held her swollen right arm against her chest the way you hold something you're afraid to drop. She had been climbing the fence behind the school gym, showing Beau and Nicholas that she could get over it without touching the top bar, and now she was the one who needed help getting down. Beau had run for the coach. Nicholas had sat with her and said, "You didn't do anything negligent, that fence was wet," which made her laugh, which made her arm scream, so she stopped laughing.

A nurse took an X-ray, and then a doctor came out and held the film up to the light. "Good news," she said. "The break is in the middle of the bone, clean through, but it didn't go anywhere near the growth plate."

Brooklyn stared at the grey picture of her own arm. "Why is that good news?"

"Near the ends of your long bones you've got growth plates made of cartilage, and that's where the bone lengthens while you're still growing," the doctor said. "A break through one of those can affect how the bone grows." She tapped the film. "Yours missed it. You'll be fine."

While they waited for the cast, Brooklyn kept looking at her arm and thinking about what she couldn't see. The break in the middle showed up as a dark line, like a crack in ice. But the growth plate was cartilage, and she couldn't spot it at all. She tracked down the doctor in the hallway and asked to see the X-ray again. "So the soft part is at the end," she said slowly, pointing to the area just below her wrist, "and the hard part in the middle is finished growing?"

"That's the idea," the doctor said.

"Then the cast has to hold the middle still," Brooklyn said, "but the end still needs to keep growing while it's on." The doctor smiled and said that was exactly why they check it so carefully.

Beau and Nicholas were allowed back for ten minutes. Nicholas brought a marker so everyone in the waiting room could sign the bright blue cast, and Brooklyn held still while a boy about seven years old drew a wobbly dinosaur on it. "It's some kind of polymer," Nicholas said, knocking on the hard shell with his knuckle. "Feels like a spaceship." Beau had already planned the next three weekends around teaching Brooklyn to throw a ball left-handed, and she said fine, but she wanted to mediate the rules: left-handed only, and nobody kept score until she got good. Beau stuck out his left hand, and Brooklyn shook it with hers.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Rotating crops, so the same plant family is not grown in the same spot year after year, helps keep soil pests and diseases from building up.
story:
Every spring, Nora's family planted tomatoes in the same sunny corner behind the garage, because that was where tomatoes went, the way the cereal went above the bowl. This year the corner was hers, all hers, and she had big plans. "Beans, carrots, tomatoes, and one mystery row," she announced to Nayla, who had come over with a juice box and zero intention of digging.

By July the beans were climbing and the carrots were feathery, but the tomatoes stood small and yellowing, with spotted leaves. Nora's dad said maybe she'd watered wrong. "I watered exactly right," Nora insisted. "I have a chart." Nayla leaned over the droopy plants. "From my perspective, they look like sad lettuce." Nora didn't laugh, because something was nagging at her. Last summer the tomatoes had been spotty too, and the summer before that. Only in that corner. Her chart said she'd done everything the same as her mother used to, and that was the problem. The same plants in the same spot, every single year, and every year a little sicker.

She flipped through her garden notebook and drew the backyard from above, like a map, then made paper squares for each vegetable and shuffled them around to simulate a whole new year without touching a single seed. If she moved the tomatoes to the far bed and put beans where the tomatoes had been, then next summer she could see whether it was the spot that was sick and not her watering. "Rotating crops," she said, tapping the map. "That's what the seed catalogue calls it. Same family doesn't go in the same place year after year." Nayla squinted at the paper squares. "That sounds like rearranging furniture for plants." "It's more coherent than your mystery row idea," Nora said, and Nayla had to admit the mystery row had turned out to be weeds.

When Alice came over in August, Nora showed her the experiment plan, complete with a diagram and the words DO NOT PUT TOMATOES HERE in red. Alice had been on Nora's case all summer about the sad corner. "Honestly, Nora, maybe some people just aren't plant people." Nora held up the map. "Some people are plant people who planted them in the wrong place." Alice studied the diagram for a long minute, then pointed at the bean square. "Okay, fine, but move the carrots next to the fence so the rabbit can't get them, and I'll help you dig in spring." Nora crossed her arms, then uncrossed them. "Fine. But only because you're taller than the rabbit."

In September they pulled the spotty tomato plants and turned the soil, and Nora taped the new map inside the shed door, where the rake wouldn't knock it down. Nayla poked her head in with two juice boxes. "One year until we find out if your tomato detective work is right." Nora shook dirt off her hands. "One year," she said, "and the mystery row is yours."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Confirmation bias is the tendency to accept claims that fit what we already believe and to doubt claims that do not, without checking either.
story:
Emilie had forty minutes before the library closed and the school paper's deadline with it. She spread the layout across the table by the window while Cayden slid into the seat across from her, holding his phone like a prize.

"Got the lead story," he said. "The Ravens' best sprinter broke his ankle at practice yesterday. Their coach already told everyone the meet's basically ours."

Alya leaned over Emilie's shoulder to read the screen. The post was from an account called RavensWatch, and it was the only source. "You're sure this is real?" she asked.

"It fits, though," Cayden said. "Their sprinter limped at the last meet. Everyone's been saying the Ravens are falling apart." He wanted the front page so badly he was already sketching a headline in the margin.

Emilie felt her stomach tighten. If the story was wrong, the paper would look foolish, and she was the editor. "A rumor that fits what we already believe isn't the same as a fact," she said slowly. "We accept things that sound right and doubt things that don't, without checking either. There's a word for it, I think." She pulled a book off the shelf behind her, a paperback about thinking tricks, and flipped until she found it. "Confirmation bias. That's the word."

Cayden frowned, but Mr. Nwosu, shelving books two rows over, glanced toward their table. He said nothing, which somehow felt louder than if he had spoken.

Emilie tested the idea the only way she could before closing. She called the community centre where the Ravens practiced, using the desk phone Mr. Nwosu unlocked for her when she explained. The woman who answered checked her schedule and said the sprinter had been at practice that very afternoon, running drills. No injury. The post was fake, probably written by someone who wanted the Ravens to look weak.

Cayden sat very still. Then he deleted the draft and rubbed his eyes. "I wanted it to be true," he admitted. "That's why I didn't check."

"You're not the only one," Alya said. "Half the school believes it already."

With twelve minutes left, they rebuilt the page around a different story: how a fake rumour had spread through three schools in two days, and how one phone call had stopped it. Emilie typed fast, her fingers cold, the printer groaning in the corner as Mr. Nwosu called out that the doors locked at six. Cayden hit print just as the lights in the main hall dimmed, and the first warm page slid into his hand like something won.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them.
story:
The bell had rung, but Matthew stayed at the picnic table with his X-ray folded inside his backpack. His arm itched inside the cast, the one that ran from wrist to elbow, and he took the film out anyway and held it up to the afternoon light. The bones of his forearm glowed white, clean as chalk marks, while everything else around them was a grey so faint it barely seemed to be there at all. Shaan dropped onto the bench across from him and leaned in.

"Why do the bones look like that?" Shaan asked. "Like somebody drew them on."

"I assumed it was some special ink," Matthew said. "Like the machine printed them. But look at the edge. There's no ink on it anywhere, and my skin is in there too, it's just almost invisible."

Shaan turned the film over, then back, and frowned at it. He had his own reason for caring: his little brother had swallowed a coin last summer, and nobody at his house had ever explained how the hospital found it. "So the machine sees bones but not skin? That's weird."

That afternoon a letter was waiting in Matthew's shoe cubby, because his friend Jesse was home with the flu and had promised to look things up. The handwriting was smudged but readable. "Dear Matthew," it said, "my mom let me use her medical book. Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them. That's the whole answer. The calcium takes the rays in, so those spots stay white on the film. The soft stuff lets them pass through. Sorry about your arm. Jesse."

Matthew read it twice, then carried the letter out to the playground the next day, where Shaan was waiting near the fence with a plan. "If denser stuff absorbs more," Shaan said, "then we can test it. Hold the film up behind your cast." Matthew held the X-ray up against the low sun and slid his casted arm between the film and the light. The white bones vanished into shadow. He moved his hand, the good one, fingers spread, into the same spot, and a faint grey ghost of it appeared, thin and pale.

"It works," Matthew said. "The cast blocks everything. My fingers only block some."

Ms. Visser came by on yard duty and paused to look at the two of them holding film up to the sun. "That's an exceptional use of a broken arm," she said, "but put the letter away before the wind takes it." Matthew folded Jesse's note into his pocket with the cast-side hand, which was getting surprisingly good at things, and Shaan was already saying, "Okay, next we test my water bottle," as he held it up to the light.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Noah Webster's 1828 'American Dictionary of the English Language' promoted simpler spellings such as 'color' instead of 'colour', which became standard in the United States.
story:
The county spelling bee was three days away, and Madison had turned the kitchen table into a war room. Flashcards fanned out like soldiers, a timer ticking, and a bowl of crackers for vigorous chewing, because her older sister swore the brain ran on snacks. She was mid-word, spelling "catastrophe" out loud, when her laptop chimed. It was Heinrich, video-calling from Toronto.

"You're going down," he announced. "I heard your bee takes words from the big dictionary. In Canada we spell right. C-O-L-O-U-R. Colour."

"That's wrong," Madison said, before she could stop herself. Then she stopped herself, because last summer flashed into her head: the two of them at the lake, arguing so hard about how to spell "harbour" that they'd missed the ice cream truck entirely. Their aunt had finally bought them cones just to end it. Madison had lost that spelling argument, too, and she did not intend to make it a habit.

"Let's diagnose this properly," she said, pulling the laptop closer. "Instead of just yelling." She typed fast, hunting through dictionary websites, until she found an old scan of a real book. "Look. Noah Webster, 1828, his American Dictionary of the English Language. He promoted simpler spellings, like color instead of colour, and those became standard in the United States."

"So colour isn't wrong," Heinrich said slowly. "It's just Canadian."

"Both of them are right," Madison said, and then she laughed, because that was somehow the most annoying answer of all. "We've been arguing for a year about a word that has two correct homes."

"Not in your bee, though," Heinrich said, grinning through the screen. "If they give it to you, they want the Webster version. Color. No u."

Madison changed her mind right there on the spot. She'd been drilling the biggest, ugliest words on her list, alloy and isotope and everything with six syllables, when maybe the dangerous words were the small sneaky ones, the ones that looked easy because her brain wanted to add letters that didn't belong. She sorted the flashcards into a new pile: Words With Canadian Cousins. Grey and gray. Theatre and theater. Each one got a sticky note: WHICH SIDE ARE YOU ON?

By Friday, the pile was three inches thick. Madison spread the cards across the living room floor and spelled them to the ceiling, to the couch, to her cat, who wandered away halfway through "pajamas."

At the bee, the announcer leaned toward the microphone. "Your word is 'honor.'"

Madison smiled so wide the whole gym could probably see it. "H-O-N-O-R," she said. "Honor."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Judgment words such as best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signs that a sentence expresses an opinion.
story:
Stella set her laptop next to the mashed potatoes and clicked through three reviews of the headphones she wanted for her birthday. "Best sound I've ever heard," said the first one. "Worst purchase of my life," said the second. The third said, "Should come with a better case." Her mother said no screens at the table, so Stella propped the laptop against the milk carton where only she could see it.

"I need to figure out which review to trust before Saturday," Stella said. "One says they're the best headphones on the market and one says they crack after a week."

Rosaly, who had come over for dinner and had already eaten two rolls, leaned in. "Trust the one with the most stars. That's my system. Also, I want to be the one who picks the movie tonight, so whatever you figure out, figure it out fast."

Stella scrolled down. One review said the cord was 1.2 meters long, which she could check against a ruler if the box stated the length. Another said the headphones were beautiful. She couldn't check that with a ruler or anything else; it just told her how the writer felt. She picked up her highlighter and marked the word best in the first review. Then she marked worst in the second and beautiful in a third. She left boring unmarked for a second, then marked it too.

"Look at this," she said, turning the screen toward Rosaly. "Best, worst, beautiful, boring, should. Every one I highlighted is a judgment word. Wherever I see those, I know the sentence is somebody's opinion, not a fact I can go check."

"So the cord being 1.2 meters," Rosaly said, chewing.

"That one I can check. If it's wrong, somebody can measure it and prove it." Stella dragged a paragraph about a counterfeit version being sold on one website into her notes. "This matters too. A consumer who buys the counterfeit gets the worst headphones even if the real ones are great. So the one-star review might be about the fake."

Rosaly put down her fork. "Wait. So your birthday money is safe, the reviews are all feelings, and I still get to pick the movie because you'll be busy measuring cords. That's a win for me."

Stella's mother brought out the last of the chicken and said that whoever finished their vegetables first got to nurture the sourdough starter tomorrow, a job both girls pretended to dread and both secretly wanted. Stella ate fast, then read one more review out loud: "These headphones should win an award."

She held up the highlighter. "Opinion."

"Prove it," Rosaly said, and stole the last roll.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The word hypothesis comes from ancient Greek and literally means 'putting or placing under'.
story:
Alexander crouched by the kitchen windowsill where his lettuce sprouts used to be. Every morning he checked his little ecosystem of pots, and every morning another seedling had been chewed down to a green stump. He had been trying to nurture these plants for the science fair since September, and now something invisible was undoing three weeks of watering. The culprit left no footprints and no crumbs, only stubs.

He called Elijah first, because Elijah's family had the most affluent house on the street and therefore the fastest internet. "Look up hypothesis," Alexander said, "but look up where the word comes from, too, because Ms. Leblanc said our boards need a section on it." While the phone sat propped against the sugar jar, Alexander heard pages loading. Elijah read out, sounding surprised, "It comes from ancient Greek. It literally means putting or placing under." Alexander wrote that on a sticky note and stared at it. A guess placed under the evidence, like a foundation under a house. That gave him an idea about his lettuce.

His first hypothesis was that Cory was sneaking in after school and pinching the sprouts, since Cory had bet him five dollars the plants would die. To test it, Alexander sprinkled a thin ring of flour around each pot before Cory's usual Tuesday visit. If Cory reached in, he would leave a handprint. Tuesday came and went, Cory ate his snack, lost two games of chess, and left. The flour was untouched, but one more seedling was gone, and there was a single small paw print pressed neatly in the white dust. Cory had changed his mind about the bet on the spot, grumbling, "Fine, I believe you're not terrible at plants."

Alexander followed the paw print evidence to the back door, where a gap under the screen showed a tuft of gray fur. He wedged the gap shut, set out a dish of water at the far end of the yard for whatever it was, and watched from the window. At dusk a thin cat crept out from under the porch, drank, and moved on to easier gardens.

On Saturday he finished his board. In the middle, in careful letters, he wrote: Hypothesis: Cory is eating my plants. Under that he taped the photograph of the paw print in the flour, and underneath everything, like a caption waiting at the bottom of a page, he added the sticky note. His mother leaned over his shoulder. "So what does that Greek part mean, putting or placing under?" Alexander tapped the photo of the paw print. "It means the guess goes under the evidence," he said. "Mine got flattened."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means a faster speed.
story:
The ramp in the science lab was propped on three textbooks, which everyone agreed was one book too many, and the marble at the top of it had already escaped twice. Liam held his stopwatch in one hand and a meter stick in the other, feeling like a defendant waiting for a verdict. Mr. O'Brien had given them the task: roll the ball, measure how far it went, time it, and turn those numbers into a distance-time graph. Liam wanted one thing more than anything, which was to beat Vihaan's line.

Last week Vihaan had produced a graph so neat it looked printed. Liam could still see him laying the ruler flat against his page while the rest of the class scribbled. "You can envy my axes all you want," Vihaan had said, sliding the paper away when Liam leaned over. "Next time, roll better." That was the deal they'd made at lunch: two balls, one ramp, one graph, and whoever's ball was faster would take the last chocolate muffin from the cafeteria, the one Mr. O'Brien saved for Fridays.

Aurelie, who was timing because she refused to choose sides, crouched by the end of the track with her phone. "On three," she said. Vihaan started his countdown without waiting, which was very like him, and his ball shot down the ramp first. Liam, being impulsive, let his go anyway, half a second behind, so both marbles clicked and clattered down the lab bench at once and the phone only caught one time.

They argued about it for a full minute, Aurelie standing between them like a referee, until Liam looked down at the graph paper and stopped. "Forget the stopwatch," he said. "We still have the distances. We roll clean this time, one at a time, and we put both lines on the same graph." They did. Vihaan's marble, marked in pencil, climbed the page in a smooth line. Liam's, in pen, sat under it. He traced both with his finger and felt something click into place, the way the pencil sharpener had last week when he finally stopped forcing it.

"Look," Liam said. "Mine's steeper." Vihaan leaned in, nose almost touching the paper. "So?" "A steeper line means a faster speed," Liam said. "Mine covers more distance in the same time. Mine's steeper, mine's faster." Aurelie tilted her head, checked the columns of numbers, and nodded slowly, the way judges do when they would rather not. Vihaan picked up the graph, held it to the fluorescent light as if the light might change something, and put it down again. "Fine," he said. "But I get the muffin next Friday." Aurelie took a photo of the graph and captioned it "Exhibit A."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A cast saw's blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning, which lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath.
story:
Nicholas had spent six weeks learning to eat cereal with his left hand, and now that the day had finally come to get the cast off, his little brother refused to sit next to him in the waiting room. "That saw is going to cut your arm off," his brother whispered, edging toward the far end of the bench.

Nicholas flexed his fingers inside the stiff fiberglass, thinking. He remembered the sound from the day they put the cast on, a buzzing roar like an angry hornet, and he remembered that the nurse had touched the blade flat against her own palm first, right in front of him. "See?" she had said. "The blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning. That lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath." He had believed her, mostly, but he still didn't fully understand how something could tell the difference between his arm and the cast.

He tested his thinking on the drive home afterward, holding the idea up to the light like a mystery novel. At the kitchen table, he grabbed Maxime's electric toothbrush, which Maxime had brought over along with Kabir and a bag of chips to celebrate the arm's return. Nicholas pressed the bristles against the back of his other hand and turned it on. His skin just wobbled. Then he pressed the vibrating handle against a stale piece of bread crust on the counter. The crust trembled, too, but it didn't break apart either, which proved nothing, and Kabir laughed so hard he sprayed chips.

"You're biased toward your own experiment," Maxime said, wiping the counter. "That's a toothbrush."

"It's a vibrating thing that didn't cut my skin," Nicholas said. "That's a pattern. Rules have patterns."

The next morning his brother still wouldn't stop worrying, so Nicholas had to prioritize: he could sleep in, or he could show a scared kid that his big brother still had both arms. He knocked on his brother's door holding two butter knives, one he spun like a tiny wheel and one he wiggled back and forth against his palm, buzz, buzz, buzz. "Which one would plow right through your skin if it touched you?" he asked. His brother pointed at the spinning one immediately.

"Right," Nicholas said, pulling up his sleeve to show the pale new arm, whole and unmarked, with the faint ghost of the cast still printed around it. "The loud one wiggles. It's all noise." His brother poked the arm once, twice, checking for hidden damage, then held up his own wrist. "So if I ever break mine, I get to pick the color?"

"Orange," Nicholas said. "Definitely orange."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Natural selection requires three things: individuals that vary, traits that are inherited, and some variations helping individuals survive and reproduce more than others.
story:
Mya spread three kinds of seeds across the picnic table in her backyard: tiny poppy seeds, medium sunflower seeds, and big dried beans. Beside them she laid four tools, a straw, tweezers, a clothespin, and a nutcracker. Her little brother had asked her last night why his teacher called finch beaks "natural selection," and she had promised to show him instead of just telling him.

"You're a bird," she said. "Your beak is one of these. Pick up as many seeds as you can in thirty seconds."

Hawa had come over to help time the rounds, and Markus wanted to play too, though he tried to dismiss the whole thing at first. "It's just picking up seeds," he said.

"Then it should be easy for you," Hawa said, and started the timer.

Markus grabbed the nutcracker and cleared out every bean on the table but couldn't pinch a single poppy seed. Mya, with the tweezers, swept up the small seeds and left the beans behind. Her brother, working the straw, got nothing at all and complained until Mya showed him the straw could stab a bean like a fork. In three rounds, each tool beat the others at its own seed, and each one failed somewhere else.

"So on one island the food is small seeds," Mya said, "and on another island it's big hard ones. Now the part that matters." She held up the straw. "If a bird with a straw beak moves to the bean island, does it get to trade tools?"

"No," her brother said.

"Right. It's born with it. Baby finches get their beak shapes from their parents." She wrote the word inherited on the back of a seed packet. "And before that, we needed the first thing: the birds aren't all the same. Tweezers, nutcrackers, straws, all mixed together in one flock." She wrote varies above it. "Then the island picks the winner. Birds whose beaks match the food survive and have more babies, and the ones that don't, don't." She wrote the last line underneath and turned the packet so her brother could read all three.

Her brother was quiet for a moment. "So nobody chooses?"

"Nobody chooses."

The neighbor's cat slid along the fence then, low and predatory, eyes fixed on the sparrows at the feeder. The sparrows scattered instantly, all but one that had been sleeping, and the cat came away with nothing. Markus pointed at the cat and said its motivation was pretty obvious, and that it had failed the survival part of the test.

Mya laughed and gathered the seeds back into their cups. Her brother was still holding the straw, stabbing beans one at a time, very slowly, refusing to quit.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome, a ticking device that sets a steady tempo, in 1815.
story:
Matthew set the sheet music on the piano stand at the community centre and played the first four bars of the piece for the third time, and for the third time he sped up without meaning to. It was like his fingers had their own opinion about the tempo. In the next room the band rehearsal was starting, and he could hear Jack arguing with Evander about who got to play the timbales.

"You're rushing again," said Evander, leaning in the doorway with a granola bar. "You always rush. Last week Mr. Rodríguez stopped the whole ensemble twice because of you."

That was true, and it stung. Matthew remembered the winter concert, the flashback he kept trying to shake off: him at the keyboard, barreling through the quiet middle section while the trumpet player shot him a look, the music tumbling forward like a shopping cart with a bent wheel. He had practised that piece diligently for weeks, every day after school, and it had still fallen apart in public. Practising more clearly was not the answer. Something hidden was going on, some rule inside his own hands, and he could not watch it happen because it happened too fast to notice.

"Maybe the problem isn't your practising," Evander said, mouth full. "Maybe it's that you have no clock in your head. Have you tried that thing?" He pointed to a shelf near the window, where somebody's wooden box sat gathering dust. A little brass pendulum hung inside it, and a sticker on the lid said MAELZEL, 1815.

"What is it?"

"A metronome. Maelzel patented it in 1815. It ticks a steady tempo. Wind it up and see."

Matthew lifted it down, turned the crank, and set the sliding weight near the bottom of the pendulum. Tick. Tick. Tick. Slow, patient, stubborn. He played the first line along with it and discovered something odd: the ticking did not feel fast, but his hands were still arriving early, sneaking ahead of each click like kids cutting a lunch line. So the rushing was real, and it was measurable. Then he tried a simple experiment. He played the line without the metronome, stopped, and tried to guess how many seconds had passed. He guessed four. The clock on the wall said nearly six. His internal sense of time ran quick, like a scale that always weighed light.

He recruited Jack from the rehearsal room to sit beside him and clap the ticks while Matthew played the dynamics, soft in the middle passage, loud at the end, and Jack's clapping held him back like a leash made of sound. When Mr. Rodríguez passed through on his way to check the first aid kit, he paused in the doorway and listened to all forty bars arrive at the finish line together.

"Somebody's found the metronome," Mr. Rodríguez said.

"Somebody found out he can't trust his own head," Matthew said, and set the weight one notch slower.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A bar chart whose value axis starts above zero makes small differences look much bigger than they really are.
story:
Easton sat at his dad's desk on a Saturday, staring at a spreadsheet full of numbers that made his eyes feel like raisins. His dad had challenged him: track the recycling totals for all four floors of the office building, add each floor's column with a formula, and turn it into a bar chart by lunch. The prize was a milkshake. Easton wanted that milkshake more than he had wanted almost anything that week.

He typed numbers into column B, then tried to mimic what he had seen his dad do, clicking the little fx button and writing =SUM(B2:B9). When the total appeared at the bottom of the column all by itself, he actually laughed out loud. "It counted them for me," he said to the empty office. "Like magic, except with math." Then he highlighted the totals and clicked Chart, and four bars climbed up the screen. Floor Three's bar towered over the others like a skyscraper next to garden sheds.

"Whoa," said a voice behind him. It was Sana, whose mom worked down the hall and who always showed up when there were snacks involved. "Floor Three is crushing everyone."

Easton frowned at the screen. Something felt off, the way a picture of a friend can look strange if it's stretched. He looked at the actual numbers. Floor Three had 96 bottles. Floor Two had 92. That was only four more, barely anything. So why did the bars look like a mountain versus a pebble? "That's weird," he said. "The numbers are almost the same."

He leaned closer and noticed tiny marks along the side of the chart. The bottom of the bars didn't start at zero. They started at 90. Easton rubbed his chin like a detective in a movie he'd seen once. What if the bars started at zero instead? Would that fix it? There was only one way to find out. He right-clicked the axis, hunted through the menus, found a box that said "minimum," and typed 0.

The bars collapsed. All four of them turned into nearly equal towers, like a row of apartment buildings built by the same architect. Sana burst out laughing. "It was faking! Floor Three looked like a giant and it's only ahead by four bottles."

"So the chart wasn't lying exactly," Easton said slowly, watching the honest new bars. "But if the axis starts above zero, small differences look way bigger than they really are." He felt like he had pulled a curtain back on something sneaky, which was ironic, because he had made the sneaky chart himself. He wondered how many charts in newspapers and on TV did this exact trick, and whether anyone ever noticed.

Just then his dad came around the corner with a raised eyebrow. "Any word on an amendment to my recycling report, or are you two just decorating my computer?"

"It's done," Easton said, and hit print.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: When David Rudisha set the men's 800-metre world record at the 2012 London Olympics, his first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second.
story:
Sara had lost the eight hundred metres three times this season, and every time it happened the same way. She exploded off the line, led the whole first lap, and then her legs turned to wet sand on the second while other runners streamed past her. Tonight, in the empty school gym, she stood at the marked indoor oval Mr. Koné had taped onto the floor and stared at the two lap lines like they were a puzzle. Something invisible was beating her, and she wanted to see it.

"Trying to figure out why you die at four hundred?" Mohamed asked, dribbling a basketball nearby. Anna sat on the bleachers with her laptop, unwrapping a granola bar and offering half to Sara without a word.

"I run fast," Sara said. "That should be good. So why does fast lose?"

"Maybe fast isn't the crucial thing," Anna said. "Maybe it's fast at the right time." She turned the laptop around. "I found the world record race. Want to watch how a champion paced it?"

They crowded around the screen and watched David Rudisha run the men's eight hundred metres at the 2012 London Olympics. Sara leaned close to the split times, and something clicked. "Look at that," she said slowly. "His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second. The fastest man ever slowed down on purpose, kind of. He didn't save everything." She looked up. "So it's not slow first, sprint second. It's just slightly less fast first."

Mr. Koné, locking the equipment cage, raised an eyebrow. "You going to test that, or talk about it all night?"

Sara borrowed the stopwatch Mohamed tossed her and ran lap after lap while Anna called out splits and Mohamed jogged beside her the last fifty metres each time, shouting that she had more left than she thought. On her first attempt she went out too hard anyway and finished gasping. "You're excited, not calculating," Anna said gently, handing her a water bottle. "Try forgetting the girl next to you exists."

The next time, Sara counted her steps through the first curve, held herself back a whisper's worth, and told herself the leader of lap one was not the winner of the race. When she crossed the second line, her lungs burned but her legs still answered, and Anna shouted, "Negative split by a hair!" Sara bent over, laughing between breaths. "So that's the factor I was missing," she said. "Not effort. Placement of effort." Mohamed held up his hand, and she slapped it, still catching her breath.

At the meet on Saturday, two girls surged ahead of her in the first curve, and for one second every muscle begged to chase them. Sara let them go. She kept her rhythm, her whisper's worth held back, and when the bell rang for the final lap she was still whole. Coming off the last bend she found another gear she had left in storage, passed one girl, then the other, and hit the tape with her arms up. Anna's voice cracked yelling her name from the fence. Sara walked over on shaking legs, took the water Anna held out, and said, "Tell me my splits."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder, the Jewish meal retelling the Exodus from Egypt, the youngest able child traditionally asks the Four Questions.
story:
The cultural center's social hall smelled of matzo ball soup and candle wax, and Sophia found her family's table near the window, right beside the ones Paris and Santino from school had saved for their own families. Her little cousin Benjie, who was seven, sat clutching a folded paper under his napkin like it was something he'd smuggled in. He had been muttering at breakfast all week, whispering in the car, and once Sophia had caught him practicing to the bathroom mirror.

"You look like you're going to be sick," she whispered, sliding into the chair beside him.

"I'm not sick," Benjie said, but he didn't let go of the paper.

Sophia thought about last year, when she had been the youngest at the Seder and it had been her turn. She remembered standing up with her knees shaking and her voice cracking on the second question, and how her grandmother had smiled the whole way through anyway. She had almost offered to take Benjie's place this year, the way an older cousin supposedly could, but she'd decided against it and still wasn't sure that had been fair of her.

She tested a theory quietly. "Is it because of the part where everyone stares at you?" she asked.

Benjie shook his head. "It's because I'll mess up the Four Questions and everyone will know the youngest kid couldn't do it."

Sophia leaned back. So that was it. He didn't mind the crowd; he minded being the one who was supposed to know. "The youngest one always asks them," she said. "That's how it works. It's not a test you can fail. Even if you skip a word, it still counts."

He looked at the paper, then at the candles, then at her. "Even if my voice goes squeaky?"

"Even then."

Down the table, her uncle was telling the story of the Exodus from Egypt, and her aunt was describing how the center had asked families to donate extra grape juice and horseradish for the guests who came without any. The horseradish, the bitter herb, was notorious at their table for making Grandpa's eyes water every single year, and by the time the plagues were recited, sure enough, he was dabbing his face with his napkin while everyone pretended not to notice.

At last the moment came. Benjie stood up. The paper shook in his hand and his voice wobbled on the first question, squeaked badly on the third, and dropped so low on the fourth that Sophia's mother leaned forward to hear. But nobody laughed, nobody corrected him, and when he sat down, Paris, three tables away, gave him a little wave.

"That was pretty good," Sophia told him.

Benjie refolded the paper very carefully and put it in his pocket. "Next year I'm doing it without the paper," he said, and reached for a piece of matzo.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
The away team's goalie had just made his thirty-second save when Nikhil leaned across the bleachers and asked the question that had been bothering Felix all week. "Okay, so a perfect passer rating in the NFL is 158.3. Why not 100? Who picks a number like that?" Felix pulled his toque down over his ears. The rink was cold enough that his breath hung in front of him, and the scoreboard above the ice showed shots on goal: 32 for one team, 9 for the other. "Somebody had to pick something," Ulysse said, without looking up from the game. "They couldn't just say he's good."

Felix could not stop thinking about it, even while the home team's best player flew down the wing and rang a shot off the post. On the drive home, his dad had the sports radio on, and a voice said that a quarterback had a rating of 112.4. "That's out of 158.3," the voice added. Felix stared out the window at the streetlights. He tried an experiment on Monday at school. He wrote 112.4 on a scrap of paper, drew a line under it, and wrote 100 under that. Then he crossed it out and wrote 158.3 instead, because that was the ceiling, the way 100 percent was the ceiling on a math test.

At lunch he showed the paper to Nikhil and Ulysse in the cafeteria. "Here's a hypothetical," Felix said. "A quarterback throws one pass, and it's a touchdown. Perfect, right? But his rating isn't 158.3, because the number isn't for one throw. It squishes a whole pile of throws into one number, like how the scoreboard last night said the goalie made 32 saves, but that doesn't tell you if the saves were easy or impossible." Nikhil squinted at the paper. "So the weird number is weird because it's doing a weird job." "Basically," Felix said. Ulysse stabbed his fork into his pasta. "This is why I like goals. One goal equals one goal."

Ms. Ho overheard the last part when she came by to collect trays. She had coached Felix's floor hockey club the year before, and she knew about numbers, too, because she kept the standings for the city league. "You three should see how the league ranks teams," she said. "People always modify the rules when one number isn't telling the whole story. It drives the parents wild." She handed them a printed standings sheet. Felix ran his finger down the columns: wins, losses, goals for, goals against, and then a single percentage at the end. The team in first place had fewer wins than the team in third. "How?" Nikhil said. "Games in hand," Ms. Ho said, and walked off with the tray cart rattling behind her.

That evening Felix did his test. He took the standings sheet home, got out his calculator, and worked out each team's percentage from its own wins and games played, not from the wins alone. Third place rose above first. The percentage had been hiding the pattern the whole time, the way stamina hides under a player's jersey, unseen until the third period when he's still skating and everyone else is gripping their knees. Felix texted a photo of his recalculation to Nikhil, who replied with a single message: "so the number was telling the truth but not the WHOLE truth."

At Thursday's floor hockey practice, Ms. Ho taped the corrected standings to the gym wall, with Felix's percentages beside each team. Ulysse looked at it, then at Felix, and pointed his stick at him. "Congratulations," Ulysse said. "You're now the kid who does math for fun." Felix picked up a ball and dropped it at centre floor. "Faceoff first," he said. "We'll settle the rankings the old way."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: A ball rolling on a flat floor gradually slows down because friction and rolling resistance take away its energy.
story:
Tristan crouched at one end of the science lab with a marble in his hand and ten minutes left before the bell. Mr. Kim had set the challenge at the start of class: measure the speed of a rolling ball, draw a distance-time graph, and have it on his desk by the end of the period. Aryan had already finished his graph, all neat columns and confident lines, and Tristan's paper was still blank.

"Want me to time it?" Zia offered, holding the stopwatch. "But I'm impartial, so no arguing if your numbers are terrible."

"Deal," Tristan said. He marked the tile floor with chalk every fifty centimetres, set the marble at the zero line, and gave it a push. Zia called out the times as it crossed each mark, and Tristan scribbled them down. The marble moved fast at first, then slower, and by the last chalk line it was barely crawling. When he plotted the points, they didn't make a straight line at all. They curved, flattening out like a hill levelling into a plain.

"That can't be right," Tristan said. "Aryan's graph is straight."

Aryan leaned over from the next bench. "I rolled mine on the counter. Smooth surface. Yours is on the floor, right by the carpet square where the stools sit?"

Tristan looked down. His chalk line ended a hand's width from the ragged square of carpet Mr. Kim kept there to stop the stools scratching the tile. His marble had rolled the whole course on tile, but the last run of the day before, when he'd tested it before setting up, had stopped almost immediately on the carpet. Why had that one quit so fast? He had an idea forming, but he couldn't quite articulate it yet.

"Five minutes," Zia warned.

"Roll it on the carpet," Tristan said suddenly. "The whole course. I'll move the carpet out and lay it flat." They dragged the carpet square into the open, chalked new marks on its edge, and rolled again. The marble crossed the first mark at a decent speed, then the second much slower, and died halfway to the third. Tristan grinned. It wasn't that the tile made the ball fast. It was that the floor was quietly taking the ball's energy the whole time, and the carpet took it much faster. On smooth tile the ball kept going a long way; on carpet it stopped quickly. That was why his graph curved. The ball had been slowing down the entire time.

He drew the curved line carefully through his points, labelled it, and dashed the graph onto Mr. Kim's desk just as the bell rang.

Mr. Kim looked at the curve and raised an eyebrow. "And what does this shape tell you, Tristan?"

"The ball was losing the whole time," Tristan said, out of breath. "I just couldn't see it until I watched where it stopped."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double with compound interest: divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate, so about 12 years at 6 percent.
story:
Parker had eleven dollars in his pocket and a five-year plan taped to his bedroom wall, and today he was going to spend every dollar at the farmers' market on tomatoes. Not to eat. His mother had said that if he saved the money instead, she'd help him open a savings account, and Parker wanted to see the actual numbers first.

He found Mr. Kim at his vegetable stall, because Mr. Kim was the only adult Parker knew who kept a calculator clipped to his apron. "If I put ten dollars in a savings account at six percent," Parker asked, "how much do I have after five years?"

"Simple interest or compound?" said a voice behind him. It was Londyn, from his class, holding a bag of peaches and grinning like she'd caught him doing homework in public.

"What's the difference?" Parker said.

Mr. Kim sold a bunch of carrots to a woman with a wagon, then leaned on his scale. "With simple, the bank pays you sixty cents a year on ten dollars, every year, the same. Five years, three dollars extra. But with compound, the bank pays interest on your interest. Try it on my calculator."

Parker typed. After one year, ten dollars and sixty cents. After two, eleven dollars and twenty-four cents, because the sixty cents earned interest too. By year five he had thirteen dollars and thirty-eight cents. Thirty-eight cents more than simple. It wasn't much, and he said so.

"That's because ten dollars is small," Londyn said. "My cousin saves for a mountain bike, and she's obsessive about compound interest. She taught me the rule of 72."

"The what?"

"The rule of 72," Londyn said. "You divide 72 by the percentage rate, and that's about how many years your money takes to double. At six percent, 72 divided by 6 is 12, so it takes about 12 years."

Parker did the math in his head. "I'm eleven. My money would double by the time I'm twenty-three." He stared at the calculator like it had contradicted him, which was silly, because calculators can't argue. "Twelve years. That feels like forever."

"That's the contradiction of saving," Londyn said, biting into a peach. "The boring years are the ones doing all the work."

Tara wandered over from the honey stall, heard the whole thing, and asked what happens at twelve percent. Parker divided 72 by 12 in his head. "Six years to double. Twice as fast." Tara looked at Mr. Kim. "Is he right?"

Mr. Kim shrugged. "The rule says so, and the rule's been around longer than my carrots."

They were unanimous, then: Parker should keep his eleven dollars, let his mother open the account Friday, and come back next week to buy tomatoes for the plan instead of the pocket. He put his money away and picked up one perfect tomato anyway.

"For research," Parker said, and paid Mr. Kim a quarter.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many places of worship, including mosques, Hindu temples and Sikh gurdwaras, ask visitors to remove their shoes, and gurdwaras also ask everyone to cover their head.
story:
Brooke spotted the problem the moment her mother parked the car. Tessa was already waiting on the sidewalk outside the gurdwara, and Tessa was wearing flip-flops, which was fine, but she was also bareheaded, which was not. Brooke had explained the rules twice on the walk to school yesterday: everyone took off their shoes, and everyone covered their head. Tessa had nodded, but nodding was not the same as remembering.

"I forgot a scarf," Tessa said, before Brooke even reached her. "I had one on the counter this morning and then my little brother invaded my room and now it's probably in his dinosaur bin."

Inside the entrance, the shoe shelves stretched along one wall, and Brooke counted the rows of sandals and sneakers while she unlaced her own shoes. "You can borrow mine," she said. "The scarf, not the shoes. My shoes would swallow you whole." Tessa laughed, which was the point of saying it.

Her mother patted her bag. "I brought two scarves, just in case. One of them is tropical, very loud parrots."

"That one's mine," Brooke said immediately.

They dropped their shoes on an empty shelf and pinned the scarves over their hair. In the main hall, the singing had already started, and the smell of food drifted down from the langar hall upstairs. Tessa leaned close. "This is like a siege," she whispered. "There are so many aunties guarding the door to the kitchen and they all want to feed me."

"That's not a siege," Brooke whispered back. "A siege is when nobody lets food in."

Colton appeared beside them with his little brother trailing behind him like a duckling. "Brooke, your grandmother is looking for you," he said. "She says you promised to help carry the trays of karah prasad, and she says, and I quote, don't hide behind your friend." He grinned. "I told her I didn't know where you were, but she looked at me like I was a very bad liar."

Brooke ducked behind Tessa, then peeked out. "Okay, okay, I'm coming." She turned to Tessa. "Watch. When they pass out the sweet pudding, hold both hands like a bowl. And if a grandma gives you a second helping, just take it. Trust me."

"Third helping," Colton said. "It's always three."

Upstairs, Brooke's grandmother pressed a tray into her hands, warm through the metal, and steered her toward the rows of people waiting with their palms open. Tessa followed with the parrot scarf slipping sideways over her hair, and Brooke reached back without looking and tucked the corner straight again.

"Hold it steady," her grandmother said.

"I've got it," Brooke said, and stepped into the line of light from the kitchen doorway, tray first.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's English, thee is the object form of thou, the way me is the object form of I, so "I love thee" means "I love you".
story:
The bus rattled over the pothole by the gym, and Logan's finger slid down the page of his worn copy of Romeo and Juliet. Ms. Thompson had assigned each student eight lines to paraphrase into modern English by tomorrow, and his eight lines were a jumble of thees and thous that refused to line up. He read them under his breath, tapping the edge of the book against his knee.

"You look like the bus ran over your homework," Maiya said, dropping into the seat across the aisle.
