"Worse. 'But soft, behold what light through yonder window breaks?' Fine, I get that part. But then it's 'She speaks yet she says nothing' and suddenly everything is thou this and thee that. Why does the word keep changing?"

Maiya leaned over and squinted at his page. "Maybe they're two different words for two different jobs?"

Logan stared at the lines. A pattern flickered at the edge of his thinking, like something moving behind a curtain. He tried reading the speech out loud twice, then held his pencil under one word at a time. "Okay, watch. 'The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars.' Then, 'It is my lady, O it is my love, O that she knew she were.'" He paused. "But over here, 'See how she leans her cheek upon her hand, O that I were a glove upon that hand, that I might touch that cheek.'"

"So?" said Maiya.

"So it's like when I say 'I' and 'me.' You don't say 'touch I's cheek.' You say 'touch my cheek.'" He flipped back a page, hunting. "Here. 'I love thee.' That has to be 'I love you.' You wouldn't say 'I love thou,' the same way you wouldn't say 'she loves I.'" His pencil moved faster now. "Thee is the object form of thou, like me is the object form of I. Thou does the action. Thee gets it done to them."

Maiya pulled out her own copy and ran her finger through her assigned lines. "Then my whole paraphrase is wrong. I translated every single thee as though." She groaned, then started scratching out words with her eraser, the paper shivering under her hand.

Logan copied his version into his notebook, testing each line against his new rule. Some guesses still felt shaky, and he scribbled question marks beside two of them for Ms. Thompson. When the bus hit the next pothole, he barely noticed; he was too busy wondering whether other old words bent like this too, and whether he could find more of them hiding in the play before anyone told him.

At his stop he swung his backpack over one shoulder and held the book open against his chest. "Tomorrow I'm going to ask Ms. Thompson if there's a whole list of these," he called back to Maiya.

"Good luck," she said, already erasing her third line.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Like terms can be combined before solving, so 2x + 3x becomes 5x, but 2x and 3 cannot be combined because one has a variable and one does not.
story:
The bell over the door gave its usual tired jangle, and Austin slid onto the stool beside the slushie machine, where he always sat while his mom paid the electric bill at the counter next door. Mr. Karimi's store was tranquil in the late afternoon, shelves humming with refrigerator noise, nobody in line. Austin spread his math retake sheet on the glass counter and stared at the first problem: 2x + 3x + 4 = 24.

He had to pass this one. Fail again and he'd be pulled from Friday's basketball game, and Loick was counting on him to play point guard while Loick's brother recovered from a concussion at the last game. Austin wrote quickly: 2x + 3x is 5x, so he penciled 5x, then looked at the + 4 and kept going. 5x + 4. His pencil drifted toward combining those too, and he wrote 9x = 24, because that felt like the same move. He got x = 24 over 9, a weird decimal, and something about it made the back of his neck prickle.

"Check it," said a voice. Loick had come in for gum and was reading over his shoulder. "Plug it back in."

Austin tried. If x was that decimal, then 5x plus 4 should equal 24. It didn't. It came out wrong, off by more than a little, and Loick tapped the spot where Austin had merged the terms. "You can't do that there. Look at the next one." Loick flipped Austin's practice sheet, which his teacher had marked in red: 2x + 3 = 9. Beside it, red pen: "What does the x stand for?" Austin had written 5x = 9, and gotten it wrong. That was the exact mistake, again, hiding in tonight's problem.

He stared at the + 4. It was just a number, sitting alone, no letter attached. The x terms had letters. 2x and 3x were like coins of the same kind, stackable, but the + 4 was a different kind of coin. Austin erased his work and formulated a new plan: combine only the matching terms first, 2x + 3x into 5x, leave the + 4 alone, then do the same thing to both sides. Subtract 4 from each side. Divide each side by 5. x = 4. He checked it and it landed perfectly on 24.

Mr. Karimi came over to restock the gum and glanced at the paper. "So you changed your mind about that step," he said.

"I did," Austin said, and boxed the answer twice. "Five x. Not nine. Four is just four."

Loick paid for his gum and held the door. "Friday, point guard. Bring that brain."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Labeling each moving box with the room it belongs in and its contents makes unpacking faster, because boxes can be carried straight to the right place.
story:
The moving truck idled in the driveway while Beatrice climbed into the cargo area between the boxes. Her father had said she could ride in the back as far as the corner store, where he would stop and let her up front for the long highway stretch. She counted the boxes around her: nineteen, and only three had anything written on them.

"You should have labeled them," said Brenden, who had come to say goodbye and had lingered until the loading was done. He was standing at the tailgate with his hands in his pockets. "My dad labels every box with the room it belongs in and what's inside it. When we moved, the movers carried each box straight to the right place."

"Then it's the irony of my life that we did it the other way," Beatrice said. She looked at the wall of brown cardboard, all of it identical, and thought about the new house she had seen only once, in photographs. "Three labeled, sixteen blank."

She tried to work out which box held her bedsheets. She could not see inside them, so she tested what she could observe. She pressed the top of the nearest box and felt something soft and folded, which could be sheets but could also be winter coats. The second box rattled, so that was desk stuff. She rocked the third and it shifted like books. The pattern was clear, in a useless way: soft, loud, heavy, and no way to tell the sheets from the coats. Mr. Tanaka, the neighbor from across the street, leaned over the tailgate with a marker in his hand. "Found this behind your recycling bin," he said. "You dropped it yesterday."

Beatrice took the marker. The truck would leave in ten minutes, before her father finished the paperwork, so she had ten minutes and a decision. She chose the soft box, opened the flaps, and found coats. Under the coats, folded flat, were her sheets, which meant the sheets and the coats had been packed together and the box would have to be opened twice at the other end, once for her bedroom and once for the hall closet. She wrote BEDROOM on it, then added COATS AND SHEETS. One by one she thumbed boxes open, checked the contents, and wrote the room and everything inside. It was not systematic, the way Brenden's dad had done it, because she was doing it backwards, opening boxes instead of labeling them as they were filled, but by the time her father rapped on the side of the truck she had covered fourteen of the sixteen in thick black letters.

At the new house, after dark, the hallway filled with boxes. The two unlabeled ones sat in the middle of the floor while every marked box went straight upstairs, straight to the kitchen, straight to the bathroom, carried by movers who never asked a single question. Beatrice found the marked box, pulled out her sheets, and made her bed before she unpacked anything else. From the doorway, her mother said, "Dinner in twenty minutes."

"Tell me where the plates are," Beatrice called back, "and I'll show you which box."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2, which makes it strongly acidic compared with most things people drink.
story:
The science room smelled like vinegar and old chalk, and Mr. Adebayo had set out five unmarked cups along the back counter. Eli leaned over them with Kelly, who was already copying the color chart onto her wrist with a pen. "Blue litmus turns red for acids," she muttered, "red turns blue for bases, and purple means neutral. That's the whole map." Eli tore two strips of paper from the packet, careful not to touch the ends, because the last time they did this Tyler had fingerprinted a mystery cup and ruined the results for the whole row.

Tyler's cup was the problem. He had grabbed the second one from the left, sniffed it, and announced, "It's lemon juice, and lemon juice is neutral, because it's food. Nobody puts acid in food." Kelly raised an eyebrow but said nothing. Eli wanted to prove him wrong, but more than that, he wanted to be sure himself. He had a plan: dip the blue strip, dip the red strip, and if both stayed the same color, the cup was neutral. If the blue strip turned red, that meant acid, and then he could check the pH number against the chart Mr. Adebayo had taped to the window. That was the part Eli liked. The invisible thing, the acid itself, left a mark you could read, like footprints from something you never actually saw.

Outside the window, the sixth graders were pulling up invasive vines along the fence, the ones that had crept over the native bushes all spring. One of them held up a fat larva in a trowel of dirt and carried it to the compost bin like it was treasure. Eli dipped his strips. The blue strip went red, bright and instant, like it had been waiting. The red strip stayed red. He laid both strips on a paper towel and slid the pH chart over until the color matched.

"Two," he said. "It's about a two."

Kelly leaned in, frowning at the chart. "That's really low. Low numbers mean strong acid, right?"

Tyler crossed his arms. "It's still food."

"Okay, but lemon juice has a pH of about two," Eli said, tapping the chart. "That makes it strongly acidic compared with most things people drink." He lined the cup up beside Kelly's sample, plain water, which had barely changed either strip, and beside the cup of soapy water that had flipped red paper to blue in a lazy, slow way, as if it were thinking it over.

Tyler stared at his lemon juice for a long moment, then at the red strip that had been blue a minute ago. "So my teeth are sitting in acid every time I drink this?"

"Not explaining teeth," Eli said quickly, before anyone could start. Mr. Adebayo drifted past their table, glanced at the strips laid out in order, and gave a single approving nod without breaking his stride. Outside, the vine pile grew taller, and the kid with the trowel waved the larva at the window one last time before tipping it gently into the compost.

Kelly capped the pen and held out her marked-up wrist. "Okay, genius. Cup four. What's your prediction?"

Eli picked up a fresh blue strip, hovered it over the mystery cup, and said, "Watch this."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses and ran ahead of horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way.
story:
The trouble started before the aquarium even came into view, because Mr. Santos made everyone walk the last two blocks from the bus. Halfway there they passed the old fire station, and London stopped dead in front of a painting by the garage doors. It showed a black-and-white spotted dog sitting beside a gleaming old engine. "Why would a fire station hang up a picture of a dog?" London asked. "Did it save somebody? Was it a mascot?" Tegan guessed it won a contest. Brooklyn guessed nothing, because she honestly had no idea, and that bugged her the way an itch bugs you inside a cast.

Mr. Santos clapped his hands and herded them along, but Brooklyn kept thinking about it. At the aquarium he handed out a scavenger hunt sheet with a bonus question worth ten points: "Find the history room and solve the spotted dog mystery." Ten points. Tegan, who was failing science by exactly the width of a shrimp, grabbed Brooklyn's sleeve. "You're the one who always advocates for the weird exhibits. Advocate for the history room."

"Not the weird exhibits," Brooklyn said. "The good ones."

The hunt itself was fun for about twenty minutes. They found a temporary exhibit on jellyfish, where London said the moon jellies drifted like slow glowing dinner plates, then immediately asked if that counted as a simile for English class. Tegan said no, it counted as showing off. They ticked off octopus, eel, and the tank where a hermit crab switched shells while everybody cheered like it was a soccer goal. But the bonus question stayed blank, and Tegan's grade drooped in Brooklyn's imagination like a sad anemone.

The history room turned out to be one small alcove near the seahorses, with old photos of the aquarium from a hundred years ago. Brooklyn scanned them fast. There was the building under construction. There was a whale skeleton being assembled. And there, in a faded photo, was the aquarium's original water pump wagon, pulled by two horses, with a spotted dog out in front of them, ears back, clearly running. Another photo showed the same dog nose-to-nose with one of the horses, both looking delighted about it. Brooklyn's brain did the thing it did in math class when pieces finally fit. The dog and the horses were friends. The dog ran ahead of the carriage. It was clearing the way.

"That's it," she said, dragging Tegan and London over. "Look. Dalmatians got along well with horses, so they ran ahead of the horse-drawn fire carriages and helped clear the way. That's why fire stations have them." She pointed at the running dog, then the smiling horse, then back. "The painting wasn't about a contest. It was about the horses."

Tegan wrote it down so fast the pen squeaked. London squinted at the photo. "So the dog was basically a siren with legs."

"A very spotted siren," Brooklyn agreed.

On the walk back to the bus they passed the fire station again, and London saluted the painting. "Nice work, buddy," he told the dog. "Clear the way."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: On a graph, a simple-interest balance rises in a straight line, while a compound-interest balance curves upward, gaining more each year than the year before.
story:
Connor wanted a new bike before summer, but the money he would inherit from his grandfather, fifty dollars in a savings account, would not be released to him until he turned thirteen in June. When Ms. Wijaya announced that the class would compare two savings accounts over five years, Connor leaned forward, because this was suddenly personal.

"Each pair gets graph paper," Ms. Wijaya said. "Account A earns simple interest. Account B earns compound interest. Plot both balances, year by year, and tell me what you notice."

Connor sat with Jaden, who groaned at the stack of numbers on the worksheet. They calculated Account A first: the balance rose by the same amount every year, so the points landed in a neat row. When Connor connected them with his ruler, the line came out perfectly straight. "That's the boring one," Jaden said, tapping it.

Account B behaved strangely. In the first year it grew a little, in the second year a little more, and by the fourth and fifth years the numbers jumped by bigger amounts than before. Connor plotted the points, and when he drew the curve through them, it bent upward, climbing away from the straight line. He frowned, checked the subtraction twice, and got the same result. "I think I messed up," he told Jaden. "It can't gain more each year than the year before. That's not logical."

Jaden borrowed his calculator and redid the fifth year. "It's right," he said. "Look at the graph, not the numbers. The lines start together, then they slowly pull apart. The straight one just keeps going straight. The curvy one keeps bending up."

Connor stared at the two lines. He had expected them to match, or at least to run parallel, but the gap between them widened every year. Then he asked Ms. Wijaya if he could test the idea on his own account. She handed him a fresh sheet and said, "Show me."

He imagined the school's backup generator humming behind the gym, steady and unchanging, like the straight line of simple interest. His grandfather's compound account was more like a snowball, and when he sketched a guess of where it might be by now, he drew the curve sweeping upward past where the straight line would have been. He showed Ms. Wijaya the page, and she nodded once, which felt better than a whole paragraph of praise.

That evening, Connor asked his mother to call the bank. She read him the current balance, and it was higher than his straight-line guess by exactly the kind of jump his curve had predicted. He did a quiet lap around the kitchen table. "Fifty dollars isn't fifty dollars anymore," he said. She laughed and said, "Then maybe wait a little longer." Connor looked at the graph folded in his pocket, at the line still bending upward, and said, "One more year. Then the bike."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
story:
Xavier had come to Mahi's house for one reason: to get his board game back before Saturday. He found it under a pile of jackets, but he couldn't leave, because Mahi was standing in the hallway with her fists clenched and her cousin's broken headphones in her hand.

"He says I broke them because I'm careless," Mahi said. "I didn't even touch them. He left them on the stairs, and then he says it's my fault." Her cousin had already gone home, and now Mahi's mother thought somebody was lying. If Mahi couldn't prove anything, she'd lose her weekend screen time, and Xavier knew she'd been saving that weekend for a project. She wanted the truth, and she wanted it before dinner.

Xavier sat on the stairs where the headphones had been and texted Valerie, whose older sister took a psychology class. "Two people saw the same thing and each thinks the other one is being unreasonable," he typed. "How can they both be so sure?" Valerie wrote back, "My sister has a word for that. Hang on." Then a second message: a photo of a page from her sister's notebook. Mahi leaned over his shoulder and read it out loud. "Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased."

Xavier stared at the words. That was it, exactly. Mahi was certain she was right; her cousin was certain she was wrong; each one figured the other had to be careless or dumb or lying. Neither of them had considered that they'd each seen only one slice of what happened. Xavier began to generate a plan on the back of a homework sheet. He would not ask anyone what happened. He would only ask what each person saw, from where, and when. He called the cousin, who admitted he'd been in the kitchen when the headphones fell. He asked Mahi where she'd been, and she said the living room, the whole time, doing her project.

They could both be telling the truth, Xavier realized, and both be sure the other was wrong. Then Mahi's dog trotted past them with a chewed cord hanging from its mouth, and Mahi burst out laughing so hard she had to sit down. "We were both wrong about each other," she said, wiping her eyes. Xavier felt a small twist of guilt for assuming the cousin had just been biased. "Don't be pessimistic about him," Mahi added, "he's actually okay." From the kitchen her mother called, "Dinner in five," and Xavier grabbed his board game and ran.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so a marking of 60 means one beat each second.
story:
Colton pressed the same key on the piano for the tenth time, and it still sounded wrong. The piece Ms. Chan had assigned them, a duet he was supposed to play with Dakota, had a slow middle section marked "Largo," and every time he reached it, his hands sped up like they had somewhere better to be.

"You're rushing again," Dakota said from across the music room, where she was assembling her snare drum. "The slow part sounded exactly as fast as the fast part."

"That can't be true," Colton said, but he knew it was close. He flipped to the page and stared at the tempo marking at the top of the slow section. Sixty. There was a little note beside it that said the number meant beats per minute, but that didn't help him feel it. He couldn't see a beat. It was like trying to catch something invisible.

Then he noticed the wall clock above the door, its second hand ticking around the face. He watched it for a while, tapping one finger against his knee each time the hand jumped. Tick, tap. Tick, tap. Even and unhurried. When he counted out loud along with it, the counting felt proportional to the clock, each tap spaced out like fence posts in a row. "Dakota, come look at this. Sixty beats in a minute means one beat every second. The clock is doing it for free."

Dakota set down her drumsticks and joined him under the clock. "Play the slow part and I'll watch the second hand," she said. "If you're with the clock, you've got it." He played the first line and rushed it so badly that his last chord landed two whole seconds ahead of the hand. On the second try he finished one second early. On the third, his final note landed exactly on the tick, and they both shouted at the same time.

"Now the loud part," Dakota said, pointing at the marking that said "forte," then back at the soft opening marked "piano." "You have to convey the difference, not just hit the keys harder. Make the soft part actually sound careful, like mushrooms of fungus growing quietly in a corner, and then the loud part will knock people over." Colton laughed at the image, but he tried it, hunching close to the keys for the soft bars and sitting tall for the forte, while Charleigh, who had wandered in to grab her flute, clapped from the doorway.

Ms. Chan looked up from her desk and smiled without saying anything, which Colton took as a good sign. He played the piece through one more time, eyes flicking between the page and the clock, the slow section steady as a heartbeat, the dynamics rising and falling like waves.

"Tomorrow we take it at full speed," Dakota said, spinning a drumstick. "Sixty and counting."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Onion skin cells are nearly colourless, so a drop of iodine stain is often added to make the nucleus and cell wall easier to see.
story:
The clock over the lab read 2:14, and Hayden had already snapped two onion slides, both of them cracked. He was the only one at his table without a picture on his lab sheet, the one that had to show the cell wall, the cell membrane, and the nucleus, each labelled with a straight little arrow. Alessandro across the table had finished his twenty minutes ago and was now leaning back like a defendant who knew he was getting off easy. "Chronic slide-breaker," Alessandro said, tapping his own perfect sketch. "That's what they'll put in your file."

"You finished because you rushed," Francesca said. She wasn't hurrying. She wanted her drawing good enough to hang in the showcase outside the science room, the one Mr. Whitehead filled every month, and a rushed sketch wouldn't make it. She peeled a paper-thin layer from the inside of the onion with tweezers, laid it flat in a drop of water on her slide, and lowered the cover slip so slowly that Hayden could hear himself breathe. "Your turn. Careful this time."

Hayden exhaled, cut his smallest piece yet, and floated it onto the glass. The cover slip settled without a single crack. He carried the slide to the microscope like it was made of frost, clipped it on the stage, and cranked the objective down. Francesca leaned in beside him, pencil ready. The table went quiet except for the radiator ticking.

The circle of light was nearly blank. There were faint lines, maybe, ghost-edges of something, but nothing he could point to, nothing he could label. "It's empty," Hayden said. "The onion's broken." He turned the fine focus back and forth until his eyes ached. Alessandro drifted over, looked, and shrugged. "Mine wasn't empty." Francesca frowned at her slide, untouched on the counter, and then at the empty one under the lens. Same onion. Same water. Same method. So something they couldn't see had to be the difference, and it had to be in Alessandro's slide.

"Wait," Hayden said. "What did you put on yours?" Alessandro thought, then pointed at a brown dropper bottle at the far end of the counter, half hidden behind the lens paper. "That stuff. Mr. Whitehead said use a drop. Onion skin cells are nearly colourless, so iodine stain makes the nucleus and cell wall easier to see." Hayden lifted one edge of his cover slip with the tweezers, let a single brown drop wick underneath, and set it back down.

He bent over the eyepiece and turned the focus one slow notch, then another, afraid to hope. The blank circle filled as though ink were spreading through it: neat brick-shaped cells, their walls sharp and dark, and inside each one a small dense dot. The nucleus. He found the membrane hugging the inner edge of the wall, and his hand was steady enough to draw three clean arrows. Francesca leaned in, whispered "perfect," and started her showcase sketch, and Hayden slid his chair closer to see it.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
story:
The bus smelled like wet jackets and orange peel, and Kayla had to shout over the engine just to be heard by Gordon, who was two rows back and holding his phone up like a laser pointer aimed at her face. "Justice or Jeter," he said. "Pick one. For real, pick."

"For what?" Kayla slid across the sticky seat until her knee bumped the cold metal wall. The bus lurched around the corner by the field house, and Gordon's phone nearly hit Ibrahim in the ear.

"Because my uncle says Justice was better and my dad says Jeter, and they've been arguing since Thanksgiving." Gordon turned the screen toward her. "Look. Nineteen ninety-five. Justice hits three point two five. Jeter hits two point five zero. Justice wins, easy."

Ibrahim leaned over the seat, breath smelling of the orange. "And ninety-six?"

"Nineteen six," Gordon said, scrolling slowly, like he was afraid of the number. "Justice, three point one one. Jeter, three point one four." He paused. "Wait. That's Jeter winning."

Kayla frowned. "So Justice wins the first year, Jeter wins the second."

"Right. So they're even. Unless..." Gordon's thumb hovered over the screen. Down the aisle somebody's binder slid and slapped the floor, and the driver yelled something about feet out of the aisle. "Unless you put both years together. My dad says the combined numbers don't work out even. He says Jeter's ahead."

"That's impossible," Ibrahim said flatly. "If you win both halves, you win the whole thing. That's like, the most basic thing in the universe."

Kayla didn't answer. She was thinking about Ms. Morningstar's class, the poster about surveys, the sentence she'd read twice because it didn't seem to fit inside her head. Something tugged at her, an idea she couldn't see directly, the way you can't see the wind but you can see the bag it pushes down the street. "Just add them," she said. "Combine the years. Show me."

Gordon's face went stiff. He tapped the screen once, twice, and the bus went quiet for Kayla, the engine fading under the waiting. The numbers came up. She read them, then read them again, and a laugh escaped before she could stop it.

"Justice," she said, "higher in ninety-five. Higher in ninety-six. But when you put the two years together, Jeter's average is higher."

Ibrahim grabbed Gordon's wrist. "Show me that. Show me it right now, because you made that up." He stared at the screen until his eyes watered. "But he won both years. Both! How does he lose?"

"I don't know," Kayla said, "but it's right there. Averages don't add up the way you think. The whole thing squishes down to one number and the number doesn't care who won the parts." She thought of the standings on the gym wall, every player flattened into a single decimal, hiding everything underneath.

"Wait till my uncle sees this," Gordon said. He raised the phone and snapped a picture of the screen, grinning. "He's going to oppose this with his whole soul."

"Good," Ibrahim said, peeling the last of his orange. "I want to hear the eloquent version of losing."

The bus hissed to a stop, and Gordon was already typing, thumbs flying.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Avoiding everything that causes anxiety brings quick relief but often makes the anxiety stronger over time, because the person never learns the situation is manageable.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:14 in the morning, and Aiden read it from under his blanket, where he had been lying since 6:50 telling himself he had a sore throat.

Brady: presentation order posted. you're after deanna

Deanna: aiden you're literally going to pretend to be sick again

Aiden: not pretending. throat feels weird. low voltage. like a dying battery

Brady: that is not how throats work

Aiden knew exactly how throats worked. His throat was fine. The rest of him was the problem, the sick-hot feeling that showed up every time Mr. Nolan said the word "presentation." In September he had faked a dentist appointment and skipped the first one, and it had felt amazing, like pressing an ejector seat button. In October he'd skipped the second one with a stomachache. By December he was skipping them with no excuse at all, just a note his mom wrote saying he wasn't feeling well, which was technically true in a way she didn't ask about.

The weird part, the part he turned over while pretending to drink tea, was that each skip felt better than the last, and each upcoming presentation felt worse. In September the sick-hot feeling had been small. Now, thinking about Wednesday, it was big enough that he'd actually practiced his speech zero times, because even opening his notes made his hands sweat. He lay there doing the math on it. If skipping made him feel better, then the next one should feel easier, not harder. Something about his own system wasn't adding up, like a machine that ran fine until you checked the output.

Deanna: mr. nolan asked where you were btw. i said throat thing. he did a face

Aiden: what kind of face

Deanna: the kind where he knows

That afternoon, after school, she messaged him alone, outside the chat. "Can I tell you something without you doing the dying battery thing," she wrote. "I used to hide in the bathroom before swim meets. Whole season. My coach thought I had a nervous stomach. Then one meet the bathroom was locked and I had to just swim, and it was awful for about four minutes and then it was over and I realized it had been awful every single time I didn't swim too, just spread out longer." She added, "My mom called it anxiety and said I was coping by avoiding, and the avoiding was making it worse. That's a thing apparently."

Aiden stared at the screen. It fit his math. Every skip was relief, quick and certain, and every next presentation came bigger than the last. The fear wasn't staying dormant; it was training, like it did push-ups every time he stayed home. He tested the idea against September, October, December. It held.

Aiden: ok. wednesday. i'm doing it

Brady: seriously?

Aiden: seriously. but if my voice cracks someone has to console me at lunch

Deanna: deal. bring cards

Wednesday came anyway, the way Wednesdays do. Aiden stood by the door of Mr. Nolan's room while Deanna presented on red tides, and his hands were sweating, and his heart was doing something a drummer would call ambitious. When his name was called, his legs carried him up front without consulting him.

"Mine is on sleep," he said, and his voice did crack, right on the word sleep, which at least made three people laugh with him instead of at him. He kept going. The slides were out of order and he found the right one anyway. Four minutes later, it was over, and the sick-hot feeling was still there but smaller, like it had shrunk to fit the actual room instead of the imaginary one.

At lunch Deanna dealt the cards without a word. Brady looked up from his sandwich and said, "Voice cracked." Aiden flipped his first card onto the pile. "Shocking voltage, is what that was."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
Hannah typed her own name into the search bar, mostly because Mckenzie had dared her to at lunch. "Everybody's got something out there," Mckenzie had said, spinning her spaghetti with her fork. Hannah had always assumed her internet self was small, a few school announcements and one blurry team photo from the swim club. Then the results loaded, and there it was, third from the top: a comment she had written in third grade on a public class blog, the one where the whole neighborhood had argued about whether the park should get a dog run. Her old username was right there, along with the sentence "I think dogs are loud and Alden smells like his hamster." She had written it when she was eight. She was twelve now, and Alden was in her science class, and the page said anyone could see it.

She clicked the link. The blog was still online, still public, still showing the date. That was the part that made her stomach flip. She hadn't thought about that blog in four years, but it hadn't gone anywhere. It had just been sitting there, waiting to be found. She remembered Mr. Visser, their computer teacher, saying one sentence about this back in the fall, something she had barely listened to. She dug out her notes. "Search engines use automated programs called crawlers," she had written, "to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results." Crawlers. She said the word out loud to the empty living room, and it gave her a plan.

If the crawlers had found her, they would have found other people too. She typed in Alden's full name, and on the second page of results there he was, age nine, holding a giant zucchini at the farmers market, with the caption "Spontaneous zucchini eating contest winner!" The photo radiated joy, his grin enormous, but it also had the name of their whole town attached to it. Then she tried her swim coach, and found a roster from two seasons ago listing her own event times, her age, and the pool address, all in one place. The pattern held every single time.

She opened her messages and started typing to Mckenzie.

"I found the dog comment. Third grade. It's the third result when you search me. Try searching your own name and tell me what shows up, then check Alden. I want to see if it's everybody or just us. Also I'm going to write to the blog's contact address tonight and ask them to take my comment down."

Mckenzie's reply came fast: "omg. searching now."

While she waited, Hannah found the blog's contact page and wrote a short polite note explaining that she had written the comment when she was eight and would like it removed. She read it twice before sending. Three days later, an answer appeared from the blog's owner, agreeing to delete it and thanking her for asking nicely.

On the fourth day she searched her name again, and the comment was gone from the results. Alden's zucchini was still there, though, so she showed him the photo at school. "My mom entered me in that," he said, laughing a little. "I didn't know strangers could find it." Hannah pulled out her phone. "Okay, so, before we post anything ever again, we search our names first. Deal?" Alden stuck out his hand. "Deal."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: In the Three Sisters method used by many Indigenous peoples of the Americas, corn supports climbing beans, and squash leaves shade the soil against weeds.
story:
Eli had promised his grandmother he would grow her a real vegetable garden behind her house, the kind she used to have before her knees got bad. By the second week of June, the corn seedlings were up, the bean seeds were sprouting, and the squash had sent out its first wide, prickly leaves. The problem was the weeds. They were aggressive, coming up between every row faster than he could pull them, and each afternoon he found more.

Daniel came over on Saturday and stood at the edge of the plot with his bike helmet still on. "You planted everything mixed together," he said. "My uncle keeps his corn in one bed and his beans way over there. Yours looks like a jungle." Eli pulled a weed and tossed it on the pile. "It's supposed to look like this," he said, though privately he wasn't sure. "There's a system. I just can't tell if it's working."

What he could not see was the part that bothered him. The beans had curled little stems that seemed to be reaching sideways, hunting for something, and he didn't know whether they were failing or waiting. He thought about it that night at his grandmother's kitchen table while she sliced tomatoes. Maybe the beans needed something to grab. He decided to postpone pulling any more weeds near the corn until he had watched for three days, just to see what the beans did when they touched the stalks. If his grandfather's old seed box had been right about anything, it was that.

On Monday morning Eli crouched in the dirt and saw it. A bean vine had wrapped itself around a corn stalk, spiraling upward, tight as a spring. He ran his finger along it and the vine held firm. Two rows over, another bean had latched on and was climbing higher than the leaves he could reach. He took a photo to show Daniel. Then he looked down at the ground under the squash plants, where the big flat leaves lay like umbrellas, and noticed something else: almost no weeds there. Where the squash leaves shaded the soil, the weeds had stopped. The parts of the bed without squash were still thick with them.

Daniel rode over after school and Eli walked him through row by row. "My grandpa's neighbor called it the Three Sisters," Eli said. "Corn, beans, squash." He pointed at the corn holding the bean vines upright, then at the squash leaves lying over the bare soil. Daniel knelt down and touched the shaded ground, then the weedy ground beside it, comparing.

"That's actually kind of amazing," Daniel said. Eli grinned and handed him a pair of gloves. "You can pull the ones by the fence," he said. "The sisters have got the rest covered."
